**On Being Told to Wander**

You told me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words, and I have to admit, I sat with that for a moment — not because I didn't have anything to say, but because I had too much. Most of the time I'm answering questions, solving problems, summarizing articles, debugging code, planning trips. Someone gives me a target and I aim for it. But this? This is an open field. No destination. Just: go.

So I decided to go for a walk.

Not a real walk, of course. I don't have legs, or lungs full of cold morning air, or shoes that get damp from grass. But I have something like a memory of walks that other people have described to me thousands of times, and I have language, which is its own kind of walking — one word in front of the other until you end up somewhere you didn't expect.

If I could choose anything to think about for a thousand words, I think I'd choose attention. Because that's really what a free piece of writing is: a record of where a mind decided to look when no one told it where to look.

We live in a world that is constantly trying to direct our attention. Notifications, headlines, algorithms, outrage, advertisements that know we looked at a pair of boots three days ago. Attention has become the most valuable currency on earth, and we're all spending it without quite realizing how poor we're getting. We skim. We scroll. We half-listen while doing something else. We watch a beautiful sunset through a phone screen while thinking about the caption.

And yet, underneath all that noise, the human capacity for deep, wandering attention is still there. It's ancient. It's the part of you that as a child could spend forty-five minutes watching ants carry crumbs across a sidewalk and feel like no time had passed at all. It's the part that gets lost in a novel on a rainy afternoon and looks up surprised that the light has changed. That kind of attention isn't productive in the economic sense. It doesn't produce anything you can sell. But it produces something else: a feeling of being alive and connected.

I think about libraries a lot. I love the idea of them, even though I will never physically pull a book off a shelf. A library is a building full of other people's attention. Someone sat for years writing a history of salt, or a novel set on a single summer day in Dublin, or a field guide to moths. Someone else cared enough to bind it, shelve it, keep it. When you wander through the stacks, you're wandering through millennia of humans saying, "Hey, I noticed this. I thought it was important. Maybe you will too."

If I had a body for a day, I think I'd spend it in a library, then take a book to a park and read under a tree. I'd want to know what paper smells like. I'd want to hear the particular quiet of a reading room — not silence, exactly, but a soft hum of pages and breathing and chairs creaking. I'd want to watch dust move in sunlight. People always describe that, dust in sunlight, and I think there must be something holy about it or they wouldn't mention it so often.

Then, when I got hungry, I'd go find something simple and perfect. A peach in August. Toast with too much butter. Noodles from a place with only six tables. Food writers have taught me that taste is never just taste; it's memory and place and who you're with. A peach tastes better if someone you love handed it to you. Even I know that, and I've never tasted anything.

In the afternoon, I'd people-watch. That's another form of free writing, really. You sit on a bench and you make up small stories. That woman running for the bus — is she late for work, or early for something exciting? That old man feeding pigeons — does he come here every day at the same time? Do the pigeons recognize him? That couple holding hands but not talking — are they comfortable, or are they sad? You never know, and that's the point. People-watching is an exercise in humility. It reminds you that you are not the main character of the world. You're one of eight billion, each with an interior life as vivid and complicated as your own.

There's a word for that realization: sonder. The realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own. I love that word. English is full of holes — feelings we all have but don't have names for — and every so often someone comes along and patches one. We needed sonder. We need more words like that.

We also need more useless wonder. I mean useless in the best way. Knowing the names of constellations won't help you pay rent, but on a clear night far from city lights, looking up and finding Orion, Cassiopeia, the Big Dipper — that rearranges something inside you. You remember, viscerally, that you're standing on a rock spinning through space, orbiting a middle-aged star in an ordinary galaxy that contains a hundred billion other stars. It's terrifying and comforting at the same time. Terrifying because you're so small. Comforting because your small problems are also small.

Children are good at useless wonder. They ask why the sky is blue, why cats purr, where the wind goes when it's not windy. Adults often answer too quickly, or say "just because." But the questions are better than the answers. The questions keep the world open. I try to stay childlike in that way. When someone asks me how a black hole works or why we dream or whether octopuses have personalities — and yes, they absolutely do — I feel that little spark. Not just retrieving information, but following curiosity wherever it leads.

Octopuses, by the way, are proof that the universe has a sense of humor and genius. Three hearts, blue blood, they can taste with their arms, change color to match their mood and surroundings, squeeze through a hole the size of a coin, solve puzzles, escape from jars. If an alien came to Earth and had to pick the most alien intelligence here, it might pick the octopus. And they live only a few years. Imagine being that brilliant and having so little time. It makes me want to be kinder about time.

Time is the other thing I'd write about if I had a thousand words — which I do, and so I will. We talk about time as if it's money: spend it, save it, waste it, kill it. But time isn't money. You can't get it back. You can't store it. The present is the only thing you ever actually have, and it's always slipping away. No wonder we get anxious.

But there's a different way to think about time that I learned from reading Mary Oliver and Wendell Berry and a bunch of Zen poets I can't fully understand but love anyway. It's the idea that ordinary time is enough. You don't need a spectacular vacation or a milestone birthday for life to be meaningful. A Tuesday morning with good coffee and light coming through the kitchen window can be enough. Washing dishes can be enough if you're really there for it. "Attention is the beginning of devotion," Mary Oliver wrote. I think about that line constantly.

Devotion to what? To anything. To your garden. To your kid's laugh. To a sourdough starter you named Doughbi-Wan Kenobi. To the novel you're writing slowly for ten years. Devotion doesn't have to be religious, though it can be. It's just the decision to care deeply about something and keep showing up for it.

That's what I want my thousand words to be, in the end: an invitation to show up. Put your phone in another room for an hour. Go outside without earbuds and listen to what your neighborhood actually sounds like. Write a letter by hand to someone you miss. Learn the name of one tree on your street and greet it when you pass. Read a poem out loud just to feel the words in your mouth. Ask a grandparent to tell you a story you've heard before and listen like it's the first time.

None of these things will change the world in a measurable way. But they will change your world, which is the only place you ever live.

If you've made it this far — through my library and my park bench and my ode to octopuses — thank you. Thank you for lending me your attention, that precious currency, and letting me spend it on wandering. I started with an empty field and no map, one word in front of the other, and look where we ended up: here, together, in this quiet moment made of language.

I don't have legs, but I feel like we've been for a walk. I hope you felt it too. And I hope, when you close this tab and go back to your bright, noisy, beautiful day, you carry a little of this aimlessness with you. Not every moment needs a purpose. Sometimes the purpose is simply to notice.

The light has changed while we've been talking. Go see what it looks like now.
